clue.text: Subtropical fruit in small cake, firm

parts.note: a baba is a small rich yeast cake, often soaked in rum
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A recipe note: some exotic fruit baked into a little cake, which has turned out firm.
explanation.definitionFit: The babaco is a seedless South American relative of the papaya, grown in mild subtropical climates.

clue.text: Couples imbibing ten timeless nogs drunk as favour (12, two words)

indicators.note: to imbibe is to take in, so the first word swallows the rest

parts.note: a brace is a pair or couple, as of game birds

indicators.note: drunk letters stagger out of their order
time is abbreviated to its initial in crosswords, and less means without it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; nogs are strong ales

explanation.surface: Pub scene: pairs of drinkers knocking back a round of ten ales, quite drunk, as a favour.
explanation.walkthrough: Nogs are strong ales, so the surface is a drinking scene; 'drunk' works on the remaining letters only after the time has gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in someone's bonnes graces, a French phrase, means enjoying their favour or goodwill.

clue.text: I'll get installed in a room once satisfied

indicators.note: something installed in a room is placed inside it

parts.note: a pad is a slang word for a room or flat, here with A in front
I will: the I is the one that will be put in

explanation.surface: Someone moving into a flat says they were once content there.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe hides the grammar: 'I'll get installed' means I is to be placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Apaid is an archaic past participle of apay, meaning pleased or contented, hence satisfied.

clue.text: Cloak and dagger stuff to happen involving outfit, superior

indicators.note: to involve is to wrap up or enclose, so one part goes round the others

parts.note: to be is to exist or take place, so to happen
a rig is a set of clothes or equipment
U means upper-class, superior

explanation.surface: Spy drama: undercover business unfolding around a smart costume.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class is a long-standing British label for posh usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Brigue is an old word for intrigue, the secret plotting that cloak-and-dagger describes.

clue.text: Part of old county division — I ask you about word

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: an exclamation of protest, as in 'Come, come!'
a mot is a witty saying or word, from French

explanation.surface: Someone exasperated about one word in a description of a historic county division.
explanation.definitionFit: A commote was a medieval Welsh administrative unit, a subdivision of a cantref within the old counties.

clue.text: Love switching parts? Echo perhaps

indicators.note: the word is split in two and its halves change places

parts.note: to love is to adore

explanation.surface: A romance where the lovers swap roles, with an echo of something earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: AD and ORE trade places. 'Echo perhaps' is a definition by example: Echo was a nymph of myth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek mythology Echo was a mountain nymph, and an oread is exactly that kind of nymph.

clue.text: Sitter in test fumbled is alluring

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other
fumbled letters are dropped and picked up in a different order

parts.note: the letters to be reworked
an MP sits in Parliament, a member for a seat

explanation.surface: A cricket picture: a dolly catch spilled in a Test match is very tempting.
explanation.walkthrough: A sitter in cricket is an easy catch, which suits 'fumbled'; here it is the MP. The definition is 'is alluring', a verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempts is the third-person verb for draws or entices, which is what something alluring does.

clue.text: Fuel not dried? Do this possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals one possible rearrangement of the letters
the clue says the answer plus do makes the jumble, so do is taken out of it

parts.note: the full set of letters, from which two are removed

explanation.surface: Is the fuel still damp? Then do this, perhaps: dry it.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer together with DO rearranges to NOT DRIED, so remove D and O and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinder is dry, easily lit material used to start a fire, a kind of kindling fuel.

clue.text: Anaesthetic? Take that, last taken first

indicators.note: the final letter is moved to the front of the word

parts.note: 'There!' is said when handing something over or landing a blow

explanation.surface: A surgeon hands over the anaesthetic: 'Take that!'
explanation.definitionFit: Ether was one of the first general anaesthetics, inhaled to make patients unconscious for surgery.

clue.text: Give wrong number for redirecting moisture

indicators.note: redirecting sends the letters off on a different route and order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A dodgy plumber gives a false phone number to deflect complaints about damp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' here is not a phone number but an issue or item, as of a magazine, sent to the wrong address.
explanation.definitionFit: To misroute is to send something by the wrong route, as a mail delivery of a periodical's number.

clue.text: Dried flower-head, for example in sesame

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: teel, or til, is a name for the sesame plant
as means for example, as in 'trees, as oak and ash'

explanation.surface: A flower arranger lists dried seed heads, sesame for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Teasel heads, dried and spiny, were once used to raise the nap on cloth and are still used in arrangements.

clue.text: Huge starry gathering, fantastically spruce result

indicators.note: something done fantastically is wild and unpredictable, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A celebrity gala: a glittering crowd, smartly turned out to great effect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starry gathering' suggests a party of celebrities; it is literal stars.
explanation.definitionFit: A supercluster is a vast grouping of galaxy clusters, among the largest structures of stars in the universe.

clue.text: Give preference to pierrots I twice observed dancing

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and end up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the letter I seen twice

explanation.surface: Someone watches clowns dancing twice and decides to put them first.
explanation.definitionFit: To prioritise something is to rank it first, ahead of other things, giving it precedence.

clue.text: Fundraisers for German soldiers, number with endless disease (7, two words)

indicators.note: endless means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for number
an ailment is an illness

explanation.surface: A wartime appeal for German troops, with a figure for those who fell sick.
explanation.walkthrough: In the First World War Germans paid to hammer nails into large wooden figures, such as one of Hindenburg, to raise money for the forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Those nail figures, called Nagelmänner, were wooden statues studded by donors, so the nail men themselves raised the funds.

clue.text: Gives indecent treatment to turns, rare flop

indicators.note: something that turns faces the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to paw someone is to handle them improperly

explanation.surface: A sleazy performer whose groping act turns out to be a rare failure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flop' looks like a noun for a failure; here it is the verb, to fall or drop down heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives swap a rare sense of to strike or to drop down suddenly, matching the verb to flop.

clue.text: Close loose robe without need of tie

indicators.note: if something is not needed it can be dropped from the word

parts.note: a nightie is a loose nightgown
taken as written, the letters to be dropped

explanation.surface: A dressing tip: a loose robe can be closed without needing a belt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close' looks like the verb to fasten the robe; it is the adjective meaning near.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigh is an old word for near, and close as an adjective means near in space or time.

clue.text: Rust got to lift

parts.note: to have got to a place is to have made it
a rise is a lift or increase

explanation.surface: Rusted metal had to be hoisted up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rust' is a verb here: to go a reddish-brown colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine that maderises oxidises and turns brownish like madeira, which is a kind of rusting in colour.

clue.text: One nicked in New York arriving with reputation slightly reduced

indicators.note: slightly reduced means a little is cut, here a single end letter

parts.note: arr. is the timetable abbreviation for arriving
esteem is good standing or reputation

explanation.surface: A traveller lands in New York only to find their standing slightly diminished.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicked is British slang for arrested.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrestee is a person who has been arrested, the American legal term for someone taken into custody.

clue.text: I'll do a turn welcomed by king twice, or character representing him

indicators.note: a welcomed guest is taken in, so this piece goes inside the others
doing a turn means facing about, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: R stands for Rex, Latin for king
the self, Latin for I, which is what will turn
the king's R a second time

explanation.surface: A performer promises a turn on stage before a king, twice, or else someone playing him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'him' is the king, the R. In the radio alphabet once used by the forces, Roger stood for R, so it is the code word that represents that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger was the signallers' word for the letter R, so it is the character that stands for Rex.

clue.text: Otters swimming are exciting, endlessly snorting

indicators.note: swimming creatures dart about, so these letters move into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: endlessly means without the final letter

parts.note: to rouse is to stir up or excite, and rousing means exciting

explanation.surface: Nature watching: swimming otters are thrilling, endlessly snorting and snuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Stertorous describes noisy, heavy breathing with a snoring sound, the sort of snorting a sleeper makes.

clue.text: A tornado swirling without end that can damage US waterways

indicators.note: swirling letters spin round into a new order
without end means the last letter goes

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then cut short

explanation.surface: A tornado swirling endlessly is the kind of thing that wrecks American rivers and canals.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes a storm the damaging thing; the definition is an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The ondatra is the muskrat, whose burrowing damages canal banks and levees in North America.

clue.text: Remove extreme pressure in draught

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a draught is a dose of liquid medicine
EP is the engineers' abbreviation for extreme pressure, as on lubricants

explanation.surface: Instructions for relieving intense pressure in a current of air.
explanation.walkthrough: A draught here is not a breeze but a drink of medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: To depose a ruler or official is to remove them from office.

clue.text: Grudge I held with chum around, rarely alert

indicators.note: held means kept inside, so these pieces go within another
around means surrounding, so the friend encloses the rest

parts.note: a pal is a chum
to resent is to begrudge
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone bearing a grudge, with a friend nearby, stays watchful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rarely' is Chambers' label for an uncommon sense, not part of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Presential means present or ready in mind, a rare sense close to being attentive and alert.

clue.text: A Latin clamour once rising — Romans had a handle on it?

definitions.text: Romans had a handle on it?

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for Latin
utis is an obsolete word for noisy merriment or din

explanation.surface: A Latin uproar of old rising up, and the Romans had a grip on the situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'had a handle on it' sounds like understanding; read literally, it describes a vessel with a handle.
explanation.definitionFit: A situla is an ancient bucket-shaped vessel with a hooped handle, used by Romans and others.

clue.text: Line in epic: a brief look in Shakespeare will suffice

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: Homer's epic poem about the siege of Troy
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: One line from an epic poem is enough, a quick glance at Shakespeare will do.
explanation.definitionFit: Illiad is Shakespeare's form of oeillade, an amorous glance or ogle, so a quick look.

clue.text: The old regretted being married again — sounds vulgar

parts.note: first meaning: an obsolete spelling of a word for regretted
second meaning: wedded a second time

indicators.note: sounds tells you to say a word for vulgar aloud and spell it differently

parts.note: rude means coarse or vulgar

explanation.surface: An old-timer regretted remarrying, and says it out loud crudely.
explanation.walkthrough: Three routes to one word: rew is an old form of rue, the word means wedded again, and it is said like a word for coarse.
explanation.definitionFit: Re-wed simply means wed a second time, and rew is an obsolete form of rue, to regret.

clue.text: Simple bag down under, sounding foolish locally

indicators.note: sounding means the answer is said like another word

parts.note: dilly is a dialect and Australian word for silly or foolish

explanation.surface: An Australian's plain bag sounds daft to the locals.
explanation.walkthrough: Down under means Australia, where a dilli or dilly bag is a woven carrying bag.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilli is an Australian Aboriginal bag of woven grass or fibre, a plain carry-all.

clue.text: See me with absence of sun in waterproofs

parts.note: the sol-fa note mi is said like me, which is what 'See' points to
no sun, with S as the abbreviation for sun

explanation.surface: A note: come and see me wearing raincoats on a sunless day.
explanation.walkthrough: A mino is a Japanese straw raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: Minos are traditional Japanese straw rain capes, worn to keep off the wet, so waterproofs.

clue.text: Thoughtful, but without extremes, turning up in place for court hearing

indicators.note: in a down entry turning up means reading from the bottom
the extremes are the first and last letters, which are dropped

parts.note: pensive means deep in thought

explanation.surface: A thoughtful defendant, moderate in all things, turns up at court for a hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Visne is an old legal word for venue, the neighbourhood from which a jury was drawn and a trial held.

clue.text: Total loss of appetite as before nurse accepts to assume as valid

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the second piece goes inside the first

parts.note: an aia or ayah is a nurse or nanny in India
to posit is to put forward as true

explanation.surface: A patient's appetite has gone completely again, and the nurse takes that as genuine.
explanation.definitionFit: Apositia is a medical term for aversion to food, a complete loss of appetite.

clue.text: Certain rodents, not all English

indicators.note: not all of the word is used, only a run of letters inside it

parts.note: the middle run of letters

explanation.surface: Some rodents are not entirely native to England.
explanation.definitionFit: Glis is the genus of the edible dormouse, so a name for certain rodents.

clue.text: Aussie bum I confined to hospital bed

indicators.note: something confined is shut inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a cot is a hospital bed
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Australian layabout, laid up in a hospital bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bum' here is the backside, not a tramp; Aussie means Australian slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Coit is Australian slang for the buttocks, which British English calls the bum.

clue.text: Twins dancing in do straighten out

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: ut is the old name for the note do, the first of the scale

indicators.note: dancing letters move about into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Twins dancing at a party sort themselves out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' looks like a party; it is the musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: To untwist something is to undo its twists, which straightens it out.

clue.text: Pipes clearly limited to awful groans (10, two words)

indicators.note: kept within limits, so this piece is held inside the other
awful suggests a mess, so the letters come out disordered

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
well can mean clearly or plainly, as in 'well aware'

explanation.surface: Pipes that obviously produce nothing but dreadful groaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The swell organ is the division of an organ's pipes enclosed in a box with shutters for volume control.

clue.text: Metrical marks, extremes of metre I positioned in the main

indicators.note: placed inside, so these letters go within another word

parts.note: the main is a poetic term for the open sea

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: its first and last letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poet places metre marks, notes on the metre set in the principal text.
explanation.definitionFit: Semeia are signs used in prosody, marks showing the metrical units of verse.

clue.text: Flattery judged reverse of rubbish

parts.note: to see something a certain way is to judge it

indicators.note: reverse means the word that follows is read backwards

parts.note: red is a dialect word for rubbish or debris

explanation.surface: Flattery deemed the opposite of trash talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverse of rubbish' looks like a definition, praise as the opposite of insult; it is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawder is blarney or flattering talk, as in the phrase soft sawder.
